You simply don't tolerate incoherence. At eighteen, as head girl, it wasn't the status you craved, but the chance to fix things. This wasn't just a job; it was a blueprint.

This drive accelerated when you left the Bar. Too academic, too solo, not creative enough. You started solving problems you'd personally encountered: Apartfrom for professionals' leisure time, Funditfrog for new parents. You even reorganised your children's school fundraising from an exclusive clique into something efficient and inclusive. At Associo, you understood the tech but left when you couldn't influence the business. You've consistently traded security for autonomy. At sixteen, travelling South America, you set your own itinerary, using your Spanish and then learning Italian. At thirty-one, you left the Bar for entrepreneurship, seeking freedom and a broader engagement with the world. You married a man who is difficult but never boring, understanding that settling would clip your wings, but also bring rewards that demanded accepting constraints.

Your thirties and forties were a period of constant experimentation: businesses, house renovations, organisational changes in your children's spaces. When those conditions vanish — as they did at the Bar, and at Associo — you simply move on.

### The Centrality of Communication and Being Understood

You think out loud. Always have. As a child, constant chatter was how you formed thoughts. Learning French wasn't just useful; it was fulfilling, loving the physical act of new words, the satisfaction of being understood. At university, finding intellectual equals made conversations stimulating. Your mother said you turned their day from black and white to colour.

Others consistently see you as someone who needs to talk through ideas, values intellectual stimulation, and brings positive energy.
